title: A life of practice, closed
hookLine: a whole life of practice in three short lines
tomorrow: one full moon holds three of the Buddha's biggest days. which three?

lines: A WHOLE CAREER IN ONE TOAST?
A CHILD KNOWS IT. AN OLD MAN CAN'T DO IT.
cards: At every retirement party, someone raises a glass and tries to sum up a whole career in one toast, and the toast runs long. A Chinese poet tried it in one question.

Chan Buddhist tradition tells of Bai Juyi visiting a monk called Bird's Nest, who meditated in the branches of a tree. The poet asked: what is the whole of the Buddha's teaching? The monk gave him three lines.
Don't do harm. Do good. Purify your mind.
The poet wasn't impressed. A child of three knows that, he said. And Bird's Nest answered: a child of three may know it, but an old man of eighty still finds it hard to do.

teach.b: Those three lines weren't the monk's own idea.

They're verse 183 of the Dhammapada, and in Max Müller's translation they read: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Notice the end.
Not one teacher's tip: the teaching of all the awakened ones. So the question has a Buddhist answer, and it fits on a sticky note. Here's the teaching inside it.

Buddhists speak of the path as a training in three parts, conduct, meditation and wisdom, and one reading lays the verse over them: not harming and doing good are conduct, and purifying the mind is the work of meditation and wisdom.
And Bird's Nest adds the harder part. The verse isn't hard to learn.

teach.h: EASY TO KNOW, HARD TO LIVE.
teach.b: It's hard to live, every day, for a whole life. That's why this block has been daily, weekly and yearly practice, refuge, few wants, a vow: not more to know, just more days of doing.
A neighbor tradition answers the same question in three lines too.

The prophet Micah, in the Hebrew Bible that Jews and Christians both read, asks in the King James Version: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"
Shared: a whole life, boiled down to three things you do, not three things you know. The honest difference sits in the third line. Micah's ends walking with God.
The Dhammapada's ends inside your own mind, as work the verse hands to you. Neither one is the other in disguise.

how: In some Buddhist communities Dhammapada 183 is recited as a summary of the teaching; in practice it is lived as the threefold training of conduct, meditation and wisdom, kept up through daily, weekly and yearly practice.

games.q: what does “a life of practice” mean?
o: three plain lines, lived out day after day
hard texts, mastered before you grow old
one long retreat, taken once and then done

games.q: the question and its answers — tap the pairs.
p: the poet who asked for the whole teaching
the monk who meditated in a tree
don't harm, do good, purify the mind
do justly, love mercy, walk humbly

s: the three lines were the monk's own summary
they're Dhammapada 183, which calls them the teaching of all the awakened.
the poet thought the answer was too easy
a child of three knows that, he said; the monk said an old man still finds it hard to do.
the verse starts with not harming and doing good; purifying the mind is the third line.

games.q: your little cousin memorizes the three lines for a temple recital and announces, 'done. i know buddhism now.' what would Bird's Nest say?
o: knowing them is the start; doing them takes a whole life.
well done; memorizing the verse is the main practice.
they're kid lines; adults move on to harder texts.
games.why: the poet said a child knows it; Bird's Nest said an old man still finds it hard to do. the lines are simple on purpose.

practice: Take out the vow you wrote two days ago and set it beside the three lines: don't harm, do good, purify the mind. Read your vow slowly, once, and notice which line it lives under.
Then let the page rest in front of you and sit with it in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: A life of practice: in Pali, bhavana, cultivation. Three short lines, easy enough for a child to say, long enough for a whole life to do.

orig.note: Pali: cultivation, practice that grows something over time.

carryVoice: Here's the line: a life of practice, known by a child, still being done at eighty. Forty-five of forty-five; the block is closed.
